introduction: The readings in this guide speak of the Kingdom of God as a condition and not a place: a life of the spirit that a person can enter now and that continues after death. They say how one enters it, by a cleansed heart and a second birth; they set its permanence against palaces and powers that pass; they picture it as a feast, a garden and a tree; and they end with glad tidings that its doors stand open. Much of this language is shared with the Gospels, where the kingdom is within, is like leaven and a hidden treasure, and is not of this world, and with the Psalms, the Qur’an, Plato, Augustine and Blake. The quotations that question it come from several sides: Nietzsche asks his hearers to stay true to the earth, Rabi‘a refuses to worship for the sake of Paradise, Tagore will not give up the world’s delights, and Job asks his question about death and is left without an answer.
questions: The first readings say that heaven is a likeness and that the Kingdom is not a place. What changes in how you think about life after death if that is so?
Jesus says the kingdom is within you, and Seneca says God is near and within. What then does it mean to enter something that is already there?
Several readings set what passes away against what remains. Which things in your own week belong to each, and how can you tell?
Nietzsche asks us to remain true to the earth, and Tagore finds freedom in the world’s delights. Do these readings ask a person to care less for this world, or to care for it differently?
Rabi‘a asked to be shut out of Paradise if she worshipped for its sake. What is the difference between wanting the Kingdom and wanting its King?
The last readings announce that the doors are open. Who, in the Gospel sayings set beside them, turns out to be inside, and who outside?

outside.why: Jesus told those who asked when the kingdom would come that it does not come with outward show: it is within you.
Before Pilate, Jesus says that his kingdom is not of this world, which is why his servants do not fight for it.
Paul also refuses to locate the kingdom in outward things: it is righteousness and peace and joy.
FitzGerald's Omar sends his soul to learn about the after-life and gets the answer that heaven and hell are in himself.
Nietzsche's Zarathustra begs his hearers to remain true to the earth and to distrust all talk of hopes beyond it. Does a kingdom that is no place escape his objection, or deserve it?
Jesus tells his disciples that in his Father's house are many mansions, and that he goes to prepare a place for them.
To the man dying beside him Jesus promises that today he will be with him in paradise.
Paul states the same limit: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God.
Milton gives the line to Satan, but it has outlived its speaker: the mind is its own place, and makes its own heaven or hell.
Spinoza taught that whatever is, is in God, and nothing can be conceived without God. Why does this reading insist that a human being is not a part of the divine?
Plato's Socrates says the soul looks at existence through the bars of a prison until philosophy begins to release it.
The beatitude makes the same promise to the cleansed heart: it shall see God.
Jesus tells Nicodemus that no one enters the kingdom without being born of the Spirit: what is born of flesh is flesh.
Blake thought that if the doors of perception were cleansed, everything would appear as it is, infinite.
Paul writes of things no eye has seen nor ear heard, which God reveals to those who love Him by His Spirit.
The Sermon on the Mount sets the order of a life's concerns: seek first the kingdom, and the rest follows.

Emily Dickinson, keeping the sabbath in her orchard, says that instead of getting to heaven at last she is going all along. Is the kingdom in these readings something reached, or something travelled in?
Paul also speaks of an order: first what is natural, then what is spiritual; the first man of the earth, the second from heaven.
This is the saying the reading explains: I am the living bread which came down from heaven.
John's Gospel speaks of the believer as one who has already passed from death to life.
Wordsworth held that heaven lies about us in our infancy, and that we travel away from it as we grow. Is entering the kingdom a second birth, or the recovery of a first?
Jesus defines eternal life in his prayer as knowing God, which makes it a kind of life and not a length of it.
Jesus tells his disciples that it is given to them to know the mysteries of the kingdom.
Jesus uses the word in the same sense: let the dead bury their dead; go and preach the kingdom.
The parable describes such a day: a man finds treasure hidden in a field and, for joy, sells all he has to buy it.
The merchant in the parable finds one pearl of great price and gives everything for it.
Jacob woke from his dream of the ladder and said: this is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.
Paul's list of the fruit of the Spirit is a list of virtues: love, joy, peace, gentleness, goodness.
Elizabeth Barrett Browning wrote that earth is crammed with heaven, though only the one who sees takes off his shoes.
Jesus advises storing treasure where moth and rust do not corrupt and thieves do not break in.
Paul gives the reason for such detachment: the things that are seen are temporal, and the things not seen are eternal.
The Letter to the Hebrews says that here we have no continuing city, but seek one to come.
Swinburne gives thanks that no life lives for ever and that even the weariest river winds somewhere safe to sea. Why might someone find more comfort in an ending than in an edifice that endures?
The Qur’an says it in two lines: everyone on earth will pass away, and there remains the countenance of the Lord.
Daniel foretells a kingdom set up by the God of heaven that shall never be destroyed or left to another people.
Shelley's traveller finds a king's boast carved on a pedestal, and around it nothing but level sand.
The psalm makes the same contrast in praise: Thy kingdom is an everlasting kingdom.
Isaiah hears that all flesh is grass, and that the word of God stands for ever.
The first letter of John says that the world passes away, but whoever does the will of God abides for ever.
The prayer Jesus taught his followers ends by saying whose the kingdom is: Thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory.
Isaiah foresees a feast made for all peoples on the mountain, where the veil over the nations is taken away.
In the parable a great supper is made ready and those invited begin, one after another, to make excuses.
FitzGerald's Omar asks only for bread, wine, a book of verse and a companion, and calls the wilderness paradise enough. What separates his paradise from the rose-garden of this reading?
The last chapter of the Bible sets the tree of life beside the river, bearing fruit every month.
The psalmist would sooner be a doorkeeper in the house of his God than live in the tents of wickedness.
The psalmist has one desire: to dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of his life.
The Qur’an gives a similitude of the garden promised to the righteous, with rivers and every kind of fruit.
Ezekiel sees trees by the river from the sanctuary whose fruit is for food and whose leaf does not fade.
The psalm calls on the gates themselves to lift up their heads so that the King of glory may come in.
The Sufi saint Rabi‘a prayed to be shut out of Paradise if she worshipped in hope of it. What is being sought at the centre of this reading: the garden, or the One whose garden it is?
The psalmist prays that the words of his mouth and the meditation of his heart may be acceptable.
Paul tells the Colossians to set their affection on things above, and not on things on the earth.
The Preacher says that God has set the world in the human heart, yet no one finds out His work from beginning to end.
Seneca thought there was no need to lift our hands toward heaven, since God is near, with us and within us. If the kingdom is within, what does turning toward it mean?
Jesus tells his few followers not to fear: it is the Father's good pleasure to give them the kingdom.
A guest at table with Jesus exclaims: blessed is he that shall eat bread in the kingdom of God.
The disciples in the Qur’an ask Jesus to pray for a table spread with food from heaven, and he prays.
Mark sums up the preaching of Jesus in one sentence: the time is fulfilled and the kingdom of God is at hand.
The shepherd psalm ends in the same hope: I will dwell in the house of the Lord for ever.
Paul tells the Philippians that their citizenship is in heaven, though they live in a Roman colony.
Jesus says he has spoken so that his joy might remain in his friends and their joy be full.
This is the saying the reading recalls: I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until I drink it new with you in my Father's kingdom.
The sages said that when three eat at one table and speak words of Torah, it is as though they ate at God's table.
Paul writes to friends he cannot see that he is parted from them in presence and not in heart.
Tennyson, old, hoped to see his Pilot face to face when he had crossed the bar.
Daniel promises that the wise shall shine like the brightness of the firmament, for ever and ever.
Jesus says many will come from east and west and sit down with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom.
Jesus rebukes those who keep children away: of such is the kingdom of heaven.
He goes further: unless you become as little children you shall not enter the kingdom at all.
Job asks whether a man who dies will live again, and receives no answer within his book. What does a promise like this one give a bereaved mother that Job did not have?
The Qur’an promises the righteous a pure wine, sealed, whose seal is musk.
Socrates told his judges that death is one of two things, a dreamless sleep or a journey to another place, and that either is good. What does this reading add to his calm?
The Qur’an addresses the soul at peace: return to your Lord, content and accepted; enter My garden.
The tax-collector in the parable would not lift his eyes to heaven, and asked only for mercy.
The psalm measures forgiveness by the sky: as far as the east is from the west, so far are transgressions removed.
W. E. B. Du Bois, burying his infant son, found himself thinking: not dead, but escaped; not bond, but free.
John of Patmos is shown a multitude in white robes who have come out of great tribulation.
Bunyan's pilgrim passes over the river, and all the trumpets sound for him on the other side.
The seer of Revelation sees a new heaven and a new earth, the first having passed away.
Dante's last line names what rules his heaven: the love that moves the sun and the other stars.
Blake asks us to see a world in a grain of sand and heaven in a wild flower.
Jesus gives the rule for where happiness comes from: where your treasure is, there your heart will be.
Paul observes that God has chosen the weak things of the world to confound the mighty.
Augustine found the cause of happiness in the same place: the heart is restless until it rests in God.
The letter to the Ephesians tells its readers that they are now light, and should walk as children of light.
Proverbs compares the path of the just to the dawn, which shines more and more until full day.
Tagore says that deliverance is not for him in renunciation: he feels freedom in a thousand bonds of delight. Must other joys be given up for the joy described here, or are they changed by it?
Plato's prisoners in the cave take shadows for the whole of reality, and know nothing of the daylight above.
Jesus promises rest to all who labour and are heavy laden and who come to him.
Thomas à Kempis calls everything vanity except to love God and to serve Him only.
Jesus warns that the children of the kingdom may themselves be cast out, while strangers sit down within. What does being counted among its people not guarantee?
Isaiah promises the faithful outsider an everlasting name, better than sons and daughters, that shall not be cut off.
Paul, at the end of his course, expects a crown laid up for him, and for all who love that appearing.
Mordecai asks Esther whether she has not come to the kingdom for such a time as this.
In Revelation the door is one that the hearer opens: behold, I stand at the door and knock.
Jesus rebukes teachers who shut the kingdom against others, neither going in themselves nor letting others enter. Who keeps a door open, and who can close it?
Luke records the saying that since John the kingdom of God is preached, and everyone presses into it.
Jesus likens the kingdom to a mustard seed, the least of seeds, which becomes a tree where birds lodge.
He likens it also to leaven hidden in three measures of meal until the whole is leavened.
The disciples at Emmaus recognised afterwards what had happened to them: did not our heart burn within us?

matthew-leaven.text: Another parable spake he unto them; The kingdom of heaven is like unto leaven, which a woman took, and hid in three measures of meal, till the whole was leavened

corinthians-flesh-and-blood.text: Now this I say, brethren, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God; neither doth corruption inherit incorruption

revelation-new-heaven-and-new-earth.text: And I saw a new heaven and a new earth: for the first heaven and the first earth were passed away

romans-not-meat-and-drink.text: For the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost

luke-great-supper.text: Then said he unto him, A certain man made a great supper, and bade many: And sent his servant at supper time to say to them that were bidden, Come; for all things are now ready. And they all with one consent began to make excuse

psalm-everlasting-kingdom.text: Thy kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and thy dominion endureth throughout all generations

john-epistle-world-passeth-away.text: And the world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever

luke-fear-not-little-flock.text: Fear not, little flock; for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom

hebrews-city-which-hath-foundations.text: For he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God

matthew-suffer-little-children-kingdom.text: But Jesus said, Suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me: for of such is the kingdom of heaven

luke-eat-bread-in-the-kingdom.text: And when one of them that sat at meat with him heard these things, he said unto him, Blessed is he that shall eat bread in the kingdom of God

isaiah-feast-of-fat-things.text: And in this mountain shall the Lord of hosts make unto all people a feast of fat things, a feast of wines on the lees, of fat things full of marrow, of wines on the lees well refined. And he will destroy in this mountain the face of the covering cast over all people, and the vail that is spread over all nations. He will swallow up death in victory; and the Lord God will wipe away tears from off all faces; and the rebuke of his people shall he take away from off all the earth: for the Lord hath spoken it

ecclesiastes-eternity-in-their-heart.text: He hath made every thing beautiful in his time: also he hath set the world in their heart, so that no man can find out the work that God maketh from the beginning to the end

psalm-house-of-the-lord-for-ever.text: Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life: and I will dwell in the house of the Lord for ever

quran-all-that-is-thereon.text: Everyone that is thereon will pass away; There remaineth but the Countenance of thy Lord of Might and Glory

nietzsche-true-to-the-earth.text: I conjure you, my brethren, remain true to the earth, and believe not those who speak unto you of superearthly hopes
nietzsche-true-to-the-earth.author: Friedrich Nietzsche

khayyam-heaven-and-hell.text: I sent my Soul through the Invisible, / Some letter of that After-life to spell: / And by and by my Soul return'd to me, / And answer'd "I Myself am Heav'n and Hell
khayyam-heaven-and-hell.author: Omar Khayyám
